WORRY GUIDE — WORK

When you're torn about taking time off work

You feel feverish, yet your hand stops before making the call to say you'll be absent. "Maybe I can manage today." "If I take the day off, I'll cause trouble for others." Paid leave exists as a right, yet every time you use it, a small guilt comes with it. Let me say this first: whether to rest is not a question of willpower, but a question of judgment that looks at both your condition and your work. This page guides you through how to line up the material for that judgment.

POINT 01

What's making this hard

There are broadly three reasons you feel torn and unable to rest. The first is worry about troubling the people around you. Your share of the work shifts to someone else. That worry itself is fair — but have you compared it with the burden if you push yourself and make things drag on? The second is anxiety about how you'll be evaluated. Will resting look like slacking off? In reality, there are fewer situations than you might think where pushing through illness is what gets evaluated well. The third is how loosely you judge your own condition. If your standard for "I'm still okay" has been raised to just before you collapse, the judgment to rest will always come late. Once you see what's behind the indecision, the judgment changes from a question of permission — "may I rest?" — to a question of material — "would resting be better for everyone overall?"

POINT 02

How to sort it out

Line up the material. For your body, there are four: fever, sleep, appetite, and concentration. For your work: whether there is anything that must happen today, and whether it's in a form that can be handed over. Writing both out, you'll find that the "reasons I should go in" are surprisingly lacking in concreteness. If you rest, it also helps to decide the form of your message in advance. That you'll be absent, the handover for today's matters, and a rough idea of when you'll return — those three points are enough. This sorting out goes more easily if you do it while looking at a card you've drawn. The card is not there to tell you to rest; it's a mirror that reflects your current state — whether you're close to your limit, or moving out of guilt. If you keep a log of the days you rested and the days you went in, you'll start to see your own pattern of pushing too hard.

POINT 03

How to read the cards

When you're torn about resting, cards that stand for "rest," "recovery," "limits," "balance," and "weariness" can offer clues.

The Four of Swords shows a knight lying down with his swords set aside. It shows that stepping away from the field of battle to rest is itself preparation for your next action.

The Hermit is a sage standing alone with a lantern. It stands for quiet time to recover, and the stance of listening to your own inner voice.

The Ten of Wands is a figure carrying more wands than they can hold. It's a sign that your limit is near, and it points to the judgment of setting things down before you take on more.

Temperance shows an angel pouring water between two cups. It's the long view: adjusting the balance between days of working and days of resting.

The Four of Cups is a figure sitting without noticing the cup being offered. It's a sign of weariness and listlessness, and can point to your mind and body running out of charge.

POINT 04

Questions to ask yourself

Try answering the following questions. Fever, sleep, appetite, concentration — roughly how many points would you give each? Is there really something that must happen today? If you pushed yourself and things dragged on, who would how much of the burden shift to? Conversely, if a colleague were in the same condition, what would you say to them? If you rest, can you use that time to recover? Once your answers are in place, all that's left is to decide. If you decide to rest, rest without thinking about work. Recovering is part of the one decision.

FAQ

Frequently asked questions

When I feel unwell, is there a yardstick for whether to rest?

If any one of these three applies — you have a fever, there is a possibility of infection, or mistakes seem likely to increase in work that needs concentration — resting is the sound judgment. If you go in and get worse, the absence will only get longer. Look at it not as "can I go?" but as "is it all right to go?"

How should I send the message that I'll be absent?

Before work starts, by phone or by the method your workplace has set, keep it short. Two sentences are enough: "I will be absent today due to feeling unwell. I've summarized the handover in a memo." There's no need to explain your symptoms in detail; if you have a prospect for returning, add a word about it.

Won't resting lower how I'm evaluated?

A short absence almost never decides your evaluation. Rather, pushing yourself and making a big mistake, or spreading an infection to those around you, leaves the deeper mark. Being able to judge when to rest is seen as part of managing yourself.

Rest, or go in? Why not line up the material — your condition and your work — and decide by judgment, not by willpower?
